claims.text: Fine-tuning minor-solute concentrations such as Ta or Nb shifts the phase-stability balance of high-entropy alloys toward a metastable microstructure.
The resulting metastable microstructure favors transformation-induced toughening.
Crack deflection and twin-assisted plasticity are examples of the proposed transformation-induced toughening mechanisms.
Transformation-induced toughening enables retention of toughness under operational loading.
Below a critical minor-solute threshold, the alloy cannot form sufficient metastable phases.
Insufficient formation of metastable phases below the critical solute threshold causes a loss of toughness.
Changing minor-solute concentration modifies the balance between stable and metastable phases.
The stable-to-metastable phase balance alters microstructural pathways for dissipating energy during deformation.
Increasing minor-solute concentration beyond a critical threshold promotes formation of metastable phases.
Metastable phases enhance crack deflection and twin-assisted plasticity.
Samples with optimized higher minor-solute levels will retain statistically significantly greater fracture toughness and ductility than baseline samples.
Samples below the critical solute concentration will have lower toughness than samples tuned to promote metastability.
The proposed behavior is expected to hold only within a narrow minor-solute compositional window, described as within a few atomic percent of an optimized value.
The proposed behavior is expected under mechanical loading conditions typical of demanding engineering applications.
The critical concentration and its interactions with grain size and phase distribution may affect the robustness of the proposed toughening effect.
